captions.text: Prime numbers are the building blocks of
multiplication.
A prime has exactly two positive factors, one and
itself.
Prime factorisation keeps a record of how often each
prime appears.
Read those counts as information about all the
divisors.
In AMC practice, factor clues may appear in a number
search, a question about possible rectangles, or a
problem about perfect squares.
In Rossmoyne style reasoning, use prime powers to
explain why your list is complete or why a proposed
multiplier is smallest.
Is thirty-seven a prime number?
Think about how far you need to look for a possible
small factor.
A factor pair always has a member at or below the
square root of the number.
The prime divisors to test are two, three and five.
If no prime this small divides, then there cannot be a
larger factor pair either.
None divides thirty-seven evenly, so thirty-seven is
prime.
The small-factor test decides the question.
How many positive divisors does sixty have?
Its prime factors are just two, three and five.
Imagine choosing the number of copies of each prime in
a divisor.
The prime factorisation is two to the power two, times
three to the power one, times five.
There are three choices for the exponent of two, two
for three and two for five.
Zero copies is also a choice.
Multiply the independent choices to get twelve
divisors.
Different exponent choices make different products.
What is the smallest positive whole number that turns
two thousand and sixteen into a perfect square when you
multiply them?
The factorisation uses two to the power five, three to
the power two and seven to the power one.
Think in pairs of identical factors.
A square has even exponents, since the two identical
factors each contribute the same number of every prime.
The exponents five and one are odd.
Add one copy of two and one copy of seven.
The exponent of three is already even.
Two times seven is fourteen.
Both primes are required and adding any more would only
make the multiplier larger.
With the extra primes the exponents become six, two and
two.
Halve every exponent to get the factorisation of the
square root.
That square root is one hundred and sixty-eight.
Squaring it gives twenty-eight thousand two hundred and
twenty-four, which is exactly fourteen times the
starting number.
One has only one positive factor, so keep it out of a
prime factorisation.
The empty choice of primes, however, does give the
divisor one.
An exponent of three permits zero, one, two or three
copies.
Count all four choices when finding the number of
divisors.
Split a difficult factor into primes.
Keep the copies of the same prime together.
Match the task to the exponent rule.
Use choices to count divisors, or even exponents to
make a square.
